claim: LPS stimulates cells functionally expressing dTRPA1 channels.

claim: No Ca2+ response was observed when LPS was applied in the absence of extracellular Ca2+.

claim: LPS-induced responses result from Ca2+ influx through channels in the plasma membrane, rather than from release from intracellular stores.

claim: LPS-induced responses in wild type neurons were significantly less frequent (9/32, 28%, P < 10–3) in the presence of HC030031 than in control experiments.

In these experiments, LPS-induced responses were significantly less frequent (9/32, 28%, P < 10–3, Fisher exact test, Figure 4—figure supplement 3E) and smaller in amplitude (P < 10–3, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 4—figure supplement 3F) than in control experiments.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,E

claim: LPS-induced responses in wild type neurons were smaller in amplitude (P < 10–3) in the presence of HC030031 than in control experiments.

In these experiments, LPS-induced responses were significantly less frequent (9/32, 28%, P < 10–3, Fisher exact test, Figure 4—figure supplement 3E) and smaller in amplitude (P < 10–3, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 4—figure supplement 3F) than in control experiments.

claim: Neurons isolated from dTrpA1-null larvae responded to LPS with significantly lower frequency (5/23, 22%, P < 10–4) than control neurons.

These cells responded to LPS with significantly lower frequency (5/23, 22%, P < 10–4, Fisher exact test, Figure 4—figure supplement 3D,E) and amplitude (P < 10–4, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 4—figure supplement 3F) than control neurons.

claim: Neurons isolated from dTrpA1-null larvae responded to LPS with significantly lower amplitude (P < 10–4) than control neurons.

claim: The subpopulation of neurons responsive to both LPS and AITC in cultures from control larvae was absent in cultures from dTrpA1-null animals.

claim: LPS stimulated a significantly larger fraction of HEK293T cells transiently transfected with dTRPA1-B (14/67, P = 0.007) compared to non-transfected cells.

claim: The avoidance of LPS-contaminated food during feeding and oviposition may serve to prevent Gram-negative bacterial infections.
source: The avoidance of LPS-contaminated food during feeding and oviposition may serve to prevent Gram-negative bacterial infections, potentially compensating for the lack of adaptive immunity in these animals.
evidence: Inference about the biological function of LPS avoidance

claim: The avoidance of LPS-contaminated food may potentially compensate for the lack of adaptive immunity in Drosophila.
source: The avoidance of LPS-contaminated food during feeding and oviposition may serve to prevent Gram-negative bacterial infections, potentially compensating for the lack of adaptive immunity in these animals.
evidence: Speculation about the evolutionary significance

claim: The sensory mechanism for LPS detection exploits dTRPA1, suggesting a broadly conserved principle whereby these channels play a crucial role in LPS detection by sensory neurons in flies and mammals.
source: The fact that this sensory mechanism exploits dTRPA1 suggests a broadly conserved principle whereby these channels play a crucial role in LPS detection by sensory neurons in flies and mammals, regardless of the particular sensory modality involved.
evidence: Inference about evolutionary conservation based on findings in flies and previous work in mammals

claim: TRPA1 channels play a crucial role in LPS detection by sensory neurons in flies and mammals, regardless of the particular sensory modality involved.
source: The fact that this sensory mechanism exploits dTRPA1 suggests a broadly conserved principle whereby these channels play a crucial role in LPS detection by sensory neurons in flies and mammals, regardless of the particular sensory modality involved.
evidence: Inference about evolutionary conservation

claim: There is evidence of an olfactory-based detection of secondary metabolites of Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Our findings, together with previous evidence of an olfactory-based detection of secondary metabolites of Gram-positive bacteria (Stensmyr et al., 2012), underscore the need to consider the function of the sensory nervous system as a crucial part of a broad mechanistic understanding of pathogen-host interactions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stensmyr et al., 2012

claim: The function of the sensory nervous system should be considered as a crucial part of a broad mechanistic understanding of pathogen-host interactions.
source: Our findings, together with previous evidence of an olfactory-based detection of secondary metabolites of Gram-positive bacteria (Stensmyr et al., 2012), underscore the need to consider the function of the sensory nervous system as a crucial part of a broad mechanistic understanding of pathogen-host interactions.
evidence: Inference from the current findings and previous work

claim: The concentration of 1 mg/ml LPS used in the experiments is likely to be relevant for real scenarios of food contamination.
source: This concentration of LPS was chosen in accordance with a previous study reporting concentrations between 250 and 800 µg/ml in water used to rinse fruits and vegetables contaminated with E. coli (Wang et al., 2011). The concentrations in the surface of the food would be therefore much higher than these values, and hence the concentration of 1 mg/ml is likely to be relevant for real scenarios.
evidence: Inference based on citation to Wang et al., 2011 and reasoning about surface concentrations
